title: Running to the tomb (John 20:1–10)
hookLine: Peter and the other disciple race; the linen cloths lie folded

lines: A PAINTING OF TWO MEN RUNNING.
NO TOMB, NO ANGEL. JUST THE RUN.
cards: In a museum in Paris hangs a painting from 1898 by the Swiss artist Eugène Burnand. No tomb in it, no angel, no risen Jesus. Just two men running at dawn, side by side, hair blown back.
One is older, gripping his chest. The younger leans forward, hands clasped, eyes wide. You can almost hear their breathing.
Of all the resurrection scenes he could have painted, Burnand chose the run. So does John. Before anyone sees anything, two friends run.

teach.h: MARY: THEY HAVE TAKEN HIM AWAY.
teach.b: It starts with Mary Magdalene. In the King James Bible: "The first day of the week cometh Mary Magdalene early, when it was yet dark, unto the sepulchre, and seeth the stone taken away from the sepulchre."
She doesn't think resurrection. She thinks robbery. She runs to Peter and the disciple Jesus loved: "They have taken away the Lord out of the sepulchre, and we know not where they have laid him."
Then the race: "So they ran both together: and the other disciple did outrun Peter, and came first to the sepulchre." Such a human detail.
Readers have smiled at it for centuries: the beloved disciple, who many believe is the source behind this Gospel, can't resist mentioning that he won.
But he stops at the entrance, stoops, sees the linen cloths lying there, and doesn't go in. Peter arrives, out of breath, and walks straight in.

teach.h: THE CLOTH, ROLLED UP BY ITSELF.
teach.b: He sees the linen cloths, and the cloth that had been around Jesus's head, not with the others, "but wrapped together in a place by itself."
An odd detail for grave robbers: thieves don't unwrap a body and leave the wrappings neatly behind.

teach.h: HE SAW, AND BELIEVED, NOT YET KNOWING.
teach.b: Then the other disciple goes in too, "and he saw, and believed." Believed what, exactly? John adds, honestly, that they didn't yet understand the scripture that he must rise.
Something shifted in him before he understood it.
And then, strangely, they both just go home. No announcement. Easter begins with a race, an empty room, folded cloth, and two men walking home not quite sure what they've seen.

how: John 20 is read in many churches on Easter morning, and in some places Christians mark Easter with sunrise services, gathering outdoors before dawn as Mary did.

she thinks the body was taken: "we know not where they have laid him."

he stooped and looked in; Peter went in first.
the folded napkin was a known first-century signal that a diner would return
this story circulates in sermons and online, but there's no ancient evidence for such a custom.

games.q: you've just heard the tomb is empty. Mary is breathless. what do you do?
games.why: "So they ran both together: and the other disciple did outrun Peter."

practice: Think of someone in your life with good news right now: a new job, a recovery, a baby, a small win. Picture yourself going to them, not walking but running, the way these two ran.
If you pray, give thanks for their good news; if not, simply let yourself be glad for them.

wordCard.voice: Sepulchre. The King James word for the tomb Mary found open at dawn, which Peter and the beloved disciple then ran to see.

orig.note: Greek: rolled up, wrapped together. the head cloth was lying by itself.

carryVoice: Your line: they both ran. Not yet knowing, and running anyway. Six hundred fifty days, and counting.
